newsitem.title: USA: LA Cty rejects Lazard Freres yield burning attack.
newsitem.headline: LA Cty rejects Lazard Freres yield burning attack.

text.p: Lawyers for Los Angeles County said on Tuesday they reexamined data from their December study on "yield burning" and are more convinced than ever that municipal bond dealers made nearly $1 billion in alleged improper profits from the practice from issuers around the country.

The Washington D.C.-based law firm of Phillips & Cohen announced the finding in an 86-page letter to Lazard Freres & Co, the subject of a lawsuit filed by a Los Angeles County issuer over yield burning.
Lazard said recently the December study the law firm prepared for its client, the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LAMTA), is deeply flawed.

Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in municipal bond refinancing deals. Federal enforcement officials are conducting over 20 investigations into alleged yield burning practices around the country.
"Nowhere does Lazard (Freres) support its complaints (about the December study) with objective, quantitative economic analysis," Phillips & Cohen said on Tuesday.
Lazard Freres' charges are a "grab bag of explanations and criticisms -- some contradictory, some misguided, most flat wrong," the law firm alleged.
Lawrence Pedowitz, an attorney with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz in New York who represents Lazard Freres in the Los Angeles County yield burning case, was unavailable for comment.
Lazard Freres spokesperson Katherine McDonough also was unavailable.
In April 1995, LAMTA filed a $14 million lawsuit against Lazard Freres, in the first court challenge to the alleged Wall Street overcharges.

Phillips & Cohen said last December that from 1990 to 1995, Wall Street conducted a pervasive yield burning scheme involving at least 80 percent of advance refundings and nearly $1 billion in losses to the U.S. Treasury Department.

But attorneys for Lazard Freres in early February sent a 43-page memorandum to Donald Lubick, Treasury's acting assistant secretary for tax policy, slamming the study as being "riddled with analytical flaws and (unable to) withstand close analysis."

Lazard Freres' law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, charged, for instance, that LAMTA's analysis is methodologically flawed because it used end-of-day spot prices and did not control for differences in average "duration" -- the length that securities are in a portfolio before they mature.
But Phillips & Cohen, which relied on data prepared by Babson College Professor Steven Feinstein, rejected the arguments on Tuesday.

"If Lazard was correct and long duration securities carried risks that justified higher prices, then duration would be a significant factor in both negotiated and competitive escrow transactions," Feinstein said.
"Lazard was wrong," Feinstein said. "The duration of an escrow porfolio does not justify higher markups, as Lazard maintains. Rather, long duration simply hides unjustified high markups."
Feinstein also said that end-of-day spot prices are "excellent proxies" for the market value of securities bought for next-day delivery.
"At any moment in time, Treasury security spot prices reflect actual trading behavior by participants in a broad and deep auction market."

"In the end, Lazard fails to disturb the LAMTA report's significant conclusion -- that Wall Street unjustifiably overcharged for Treasury securities sold to municipal defeasance escrows," Phillips & Cohen said.
"As a result of this longstanding fraud, it is estimated that the federal, state and local governments suffered close to $1 billion in damages," the lawfirm alleged.
